items.prompt: State what is meant by the focus of an earthquake.
items.canonical_answer: The point underground where the earthquake starts, where the rock first breaks and the energy is released.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - the underground point where the earthquake begins. "Where the earthquake happens" alone is not enough, because the term fixes the point below the surface.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why strato-volcanoes are steep-sided and shield volcanoes are gently sloping.
items.canonical_answer: Strato-volcanoes are built of sticky lava, which sets where it lands, so layers of ash and lava pile up close to the vent into a steep cone. Shield volcanoes are built of runny lava, which flows a long way before it sets, which spreads each eruption far and wide, so the mountain grows into a low, gently sloping form.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: sticky lava sets quickly, so it builds a steep cone near the vent; runny lava travels far because it stays fluid; the two behaviours cause the different shapes, which is why the slopes differ.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
The table gives details of two earthquakes:

| earthquake | magnitude | depth of focus | distance from nearest city |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 6.8 | 10 km | 20 km |
| B | 5.1 | 55 km | 150 km |

Describe what the table suggests about which earthquake is likely to cause the more serious damage.
items.canonical_answer: Earthquake A is likely to cause the more serious damage. Its magnitude is higher, 6.8 against 5.1, which means it releases far more energy. Its focus is much shallower, 10 kilometres against 55 kilometres, so the shaking reaches the surface more strongly, and it lies only 20 kilometres from a city against 150 kilometres for B. The pattern shown is that the larger, shallower, nearer event threatens people far more.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table - earthquake A the more dangerous of the two (1 mark).
Values: the paired figures with their units, such as 6.8 against 5.1 in magnitude and 10 km against 55 km in depth, so the figures support the choice (1 mark each for two pairs).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A photograph shows a volcano with a steep symmetrical cone. Bands of grey ash lie between darker layers of rock, and a narrow crater sits at the summit. Suggest the type of volcano shown and two reasons for your choice.
items.canonical_answer: The photograph suggests a strato-volcano, a composite cone. The cone is steep and built of alternating layers of ash and lava, because sticky lava and ash pile up near the vent instead of flowing far; the narrow summit crater also matches a composite cone, whereas a shield volcano would spread into a wide, gentle form.
marking_guidance: This resource suggests 1 mark for naming the type, a strato-volcano, and 1 mark each for two reasons taken from the figure: the steep layered cone, because sticky lava and ash build steep slopes; the narrow summit crater, which fits a composite cone.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The epicentre of the earthquake is the point underground where the shaking starts." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is swapping the two terms: the point underground where an earthquake starts is the focus, while the epicentre is the point on the surface directly above the focus, where the shaking is usually felt most strongly. The test is position - underground or at the surface?
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - the two terms are not the same; the underground point is in fact the focus, and the epicentre lies on the surface above it.
1 mark: the correct idea instead - focus underground, epicentre at the surface directly above.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Describe two features of the world distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes.
items.canonical_answer: They lie in long, narrow belts along plate boundaries rather than scattered anywhere. Most cluster around the Pacific Ocean - the Pacific Ring of Fire - while the interiors of plates, far from any boundary, usually have few earthquakes and no volcanoes.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all: narrow belts along boundaries; the Pacific cluster; the quiet plate interiors; any valid characteristic of the distribution.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain why conservative plate boundaries produce earthquakes but no volcanoes.
items.canonical_answer: At a conservative boundary the plates slide past each other, and their rough edges snag. Stress builds as the plates push, which causes the rock to fracture suddenly and release energy as an earthquake. No plate is destroyed and no gap opens for magma, so no molten rock reaches the surface, and without rising magma there can be no eruption.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: the plates slide past each other and snag, so stress builds; the sudden fracture releases the stored energy, which causes the shaking; no magma rises because no plate is subducted or pulled apart, so there are no volcanoes.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
The table shows where 1,400 of the world's active volcanoes lie:

| setting | number of volcanoes |
|---|---|
| around the Pacific Ocean | 1,050 |
| along the belt from the Mediterranean to East Asia | 180 |
| along the mid-ocean ridges, including the Atlantic | 120 |
| in the interiors of plates | 50 |

Describe the pattern the table shows.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows the active volcanoes clustered above all around the Pacific Ocean: 1,050 of the 1,400, about three in every four. The rest lie in other narrow belts, 180 along the chain from the Mediterranean to East Asia and 120 along the mid-ocean ridges, while a small remainder, 50, sits far from any boundary. The pattern shown is therefore volcanoes in belts along plate boundaries, with the greatest concentration around the Pacific and gaps in the plate interiors.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table - volcanoes concentrated in belts, above all around the Pacific (1 mark).
Values: the figures quoted with their settings, 1,050 of 1,400 around the Pacific and only 50 in the interiors, so the figures support the description (1 mark each for two uses).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "The plate boundary near the coast is moving towards the continent, which is why the volcanoes appear there." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is making the boundary the moving thing: a plate boundary is the line where two moving plates meet, not a travelling object. The plate itself moves towards the continent, and where it converges with another plate the boundary between them marks where they meet. The test is to ask what moves, and which way: plates move; the boundary is where they meet, and the kind of meeting - constructive, destructive or conservative - sets the hazards found there.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - the boundary does not move; the plates do, and a boundary is not the same as a plate.
1 mark: the correct idea instead - name what moves and the direction, such as a plate converging at a destructive boundary.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Asked to describe the distribution of the world's earthquakes, a learner writes only: "They occur on plate boundaries." Explain what is missing.
items.canonical_answer: The statement is true but describes no pattern, which means it cannot carry a description of a distribution by itself. A distribution answer says where the events are, in long narrow belts; how they are grouped, clustered most thickly around the Pacific, the Ring of Fire; and where they are not, the quiet plate interiors. The test is whether the answer names where, how spread out and where not.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error - a single statement "on plate boundaries" describes no pattern; in fact a distribution needs belts, clusters and gaps.
1 mark: the correct idea instead - narrow belts, the Pacific cluster and the quiet plate interiors.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Describe two beneficial effects that volcanic eruptions can have on people and the environment.
items.canonical_answer: Fresh ash weathers into fertile soil, so farms on volcano slopes raise good crops, which feeds the families who live there. Volcanic heat also supplies geothermal energy: steam drawn from hot underground rock warms homes and generates electricity without burning fuel.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per benefit, 2 in all: fertile soil from ash; geothermal energy; each benefit is an opportunity the eruption's effects create, taken to its consequence with because or so or which means.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Describe two problems that the effects of earthquakes cause for people.
items.canonical_answer: Buildings collapse under the shaking, which crushes or traps the people inside and leaves families homeless. Burst gas pipes and electricity lines start fires that spread through the rubble, so survivors can lose their homes a second time even after the shaking stops.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per problem, 2 in all: collapsed buildings with their casualties and homelessness; fires from burst pipes; landslides; sea waves - each problem is taken to its consequence with because or so or which means.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain how movement at a destructive plate boundary can end in a damaged city far from any volcano.
items.canonical_answer: The cause is the collision: an oceanic plate is forced down into the mantle beneath a continent, and the two plates snag instead of sliding smoothly. Stress builds in the locked rocks until they fracture, so the stored energy races out as seismic waves from the focus. The effect arrives at the surface: the ground shakes hardest near the epicentre, and buildings in a city above collapse or catch fire, which means the city's damage is the last link of a chain that began with plate movement.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the cause - subduction and snagging at a destructive boundary.
1 mark for the connecting step, so the built-up stress is released by fracturing rock as seismic waves.
1 mark for the effect - shaking near the epicentre damages the city, the consequence of the chain.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
The table shows the reported effects of two earthquakes of similar magnitude:

| | earthquake in country X | earthquake in country Y |
|---|---|---|
| deaths | 143 | 8,900 |
| homes destroyed | about 12,000 | about 600,000 |
| people made homeless | about 40,000 | about 2,000,000 |

Describe the contrast the table shows.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows country Y suffering on a far greater scale: about 8,900 deaths against 143, roughly 600,000 homes destroyed against about 12,000, and about 2,000,000 people made homeless against about 40,000. The pattern shown is that a similar size of shaking kills and displaces far more people in Y than in X, which suggests the buildings and the readiness of the two places differ.
marking_guidance: Reading: the contrast read from the table - the effects in country Y many times heavier (1 mark).
Values: the paired figures quoted with their units, such as 8,900 against 143 deaths, so the figures carry the comparison (1 mark each for a further pair or the suggested reason).

items.prompt: A description of a village 8 kilometres downwind of an erupting volcano reads: grey ash lies 10 centimetres deep on the roofs, the grass for the cattle is grey with ash, cars creep with headlights on at midday, and people cough as they carry water indoors. Suggest three problems the ash is causing.
items.canonical_answer: The weight of wet ash can crush weak roofs, because 10 centimetres of ash over a roof is a heavy load. The ash-covered grass may poison or starve the cattle, which threatens the families' milk and meat. The thick air and darkness harm breathing and make travel dangerous, so people struggle to work, fetch water or reach help.
marking_guidance: This resource suggests 1 mark per problem, to 3: roof collapse under the weight of the ash; livestock losing their feed; breathing difficulties and dark driving conditions - each problem is drawn from the description given, so the answer is tied to the figure.

items.prompt: Describe two opportunities a volcano offers to people who live nearby.
items.canonical_answer: The ash weathers into fertile soil, so farms on the lower slopes produce good harvests of crops. The volcano also draws tourists who want to see the crater and lava fields, which means jobs and income for local guides, guesthouses and food sellers.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per benefit, 2 in all: fertile soil; tourism; geothermal energy; stone or sand - each opportunity taken to its consequence with because or so or which means.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Describe two hazards a strato-volcano presents to people living on its slopes.
items.canonical_answer: Pyroclastic flows of hot gas, ash and rock sweep down the slopes at speed, which destroys everything in their path within minutes. Thick falls of ash also pile on roofs and bury crops, so buildings can collapse and harvests are lost even far from the vent.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per hazard, 2 in all: pyroclastic flows; ash falls; lava flows; lahars; gases - each hazard taken to its consequence with because or so or which means.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt: Explain how a storm on an erupting volcano can end in villages being buried in mud.
items.canonical_answer: The cause is loose ash: eruptions blanket the slopes with thick, loose material that has not yet grown a cover of plants. Heavy rain falls faster than the ash can absorb it, so the water mixes with ash and rubble into a dense flowing mud, which is called a lahar. The effect strikes downhill: the lahar follows valleys at speed and buries the villages on their floors, a consequence that can kill more people than the eruption itself.
marking_guidance: 1 mark for the cause - loose ash left on the slopes by the eruption.
1 mark for the connecting step, so rain turns the ash to a lahar that flows down the valleys.
1 mark for the effect - villages on the valley floors are buried, the impact of the mudflow.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
The table shows a survey of settlements around a volcano, by distance from the crater:

| distance from crater | average depth of ash from the last eruption | number of settlements |
|---|---|---|
| under 5 km | about 40 cm | 2 |
| 5 to 10 km | about 12 cm | 14 |
| over 10 km | about 2 cm | 31 |

Describe the pattern shown and what it suggests about the hazard.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows ash thinning with distance - about 40 centimetres within 5 kilometres, about 12 centimetres from 5 to 10 kilometres, about 2 centimetres beyond - while settlement does the opposite: 31 of the 47 settlements lie beyond 10 kilometres, against 2 within 5 kilometres. The pattern shown suggests people mostly avoid the highest-risk ground, so the hazard falls with distance from the crater and settlement follows the safer ground.
marking_guidance: Reading: the inverse pattern read from the table - ash thins and settlement thickens with distance (1 mark).
Values: the figures with their units, such as 40 cm against 2 cm and 31 of 47 settlements beyond 10 km, so the figures support the words (1 mark each for two uses).

items.prompt: A photograph looks across a volcano's lower slopes: green terraces of vegetables and fruit trees grow in dark soil, a road climbs past a hot spring where bathers soak, and signboards advertise guided walks to the crater viewpoint. Suggest three reasons why people choose to live and work on these slopes.
items.canonical_answer: The dark soil is volcanic ash broken down over the years, which suggests fertile farmland and good harvests - the terraces in the photograph show the benefit in use. The hot spring and the crater walks draw visitors, so guiding, lodging and food-selling give families an income besides farming. The hot spring also suggests heat drawn from the volcano itself, which can warm homes and greenhouses cheaply to run.
marking_guidance: This resource suggests 1 mark per reason, to 3: fertile ash soil farmed in terraces, because ash weathers into productive ground; tourism from the hot spring and the crater walks, so families earn from visitors; geothermal heat warming homes and greenhouses.

items.prompt: Asked for the problems of living near a volcano, a learner writes: "The soil is very fertile and tourists bring money to the area." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has answered the opposite side of the question: fertile soil and tourist income are benefits, whereas the question asks for problems. The problems of living near a volcano are its hazards - lava flows, pyroclastic flows, ash falls, lahars and gases - which destroy homes, crops and lives. The test is to check which side the question asks for, problems or benefits.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - benefits are not the same as the problems asked for; in fact the answer lists opportunities instead of hazards.
1 mark: the correct idea - the hazards named in place of them, such as lava flows, ash falls or lahars.

items.prompt: A town lies on the lower slopes of a volcano. For a week the local observatory has recorded swarms of small earthquakes, gas has begun to rise from the crater, and the mountainside has measurably swollen. Suggest three actions the authorities should take.
items.canonical_answer: They should watch the volcano more closely, because earthquake swarms, rising gas and swelling ground are the classic signs of magma moving up. They should warn the townspeople at once and prepare evacuation routes, so people know what to do before an eruption begins. And they should move people off the highest-risk slopes and valley floors, which means acting on the warning rather than waiting for certainty.
marking_guidance: This example suggests 1 mark per action, to 3: intensified monitoring of the warning signs; public warnings issued, so people are ready; evacuation of the riskiest ground, because the signs show rising magma.

items.prompt: A district has money for one safety project: reinforcing the primary school's buildings, or buying a volcano monitoring network. Suggest which project the district should choose, and justify your decision.
items.canonical_answer: The district should reinforce the school buildings. The judgement rests on what saves lives in the town: monitoring warns of eruptions, but a warning cannot help unless people have somewhere safe to go, whereas reinforced concrete frames and deep foundations keep the classrooms standing through the shaking, because the building itself becomes the protection. The evidence from real events points the same way - in the Nepal earthquake of 2015, weak buildings were a main reason nearly 9,000 people died, which means strengthening structures attacks the deadliest part of the risk first.
marking_guidance: Judgement: 1 mark for the decision named - reinforce the buildings.
Reasoning: 1 mark because the argument weighs what a warning can and cannot do against what a strengthened building does.
Evidence: 1 mark for the example or figures used, such as the 2015 Nepal earthquake and its near-9,000 deaths from weak buildings.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 2.1 claim ledger.

items.prompt:
The table shows the earthquake preparations of two towns in the same country:

| preparation | town A | town B |
|---|---|---|
| buildings with reinforced frames | 70 per cent | 8 per cent |
| emergency drills each year | 2 | 0 |
| trained emergency teams | yes | no |
| hospital beds per 1,000 people | 4 | 1.2 |

Describe the differences shown, and what they suggest about each town's readiness.
items.canonical_answer: Town A is prepared on every measure: 70 per cent of its buildings have reinforced frames against 8 per cent, it runs two emergency drills a year where B runs none, it has trained emergency teams where B has none, and it has 4 hospital beds per 1,000 people against 1.2. The pattern shown suggests town A would suffer far less in the same earthquake, which means readiness, not luck, decides much of the outcome.
marking_guidance: Reading: the pattern read from the table - town A prepared on all four measures (1 mark).
Values: the figures quoted with their units, such as 70 per cent against 8 per cent and 4 against 1.2 beds per 1,000, so the figures support the contrast (1 mark each for two pairs).

items.prompt: A learner writes: "Fewer people died in the second earthquake because the country is more developed and has better infrastructure." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The error is vagueness: "better infrastructure" says nothing about what was actually built or done, so the explanation explains nothing. An answer must name the differences exactly - reinforced concrete or steel frames, deep foundations, strict building regulations, trained emergency services, warning systems and drills. The test is whether the reader could say what was built or done differently; a vague phrase does not pass that test.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - vague terms wrongly stand in for an explanation; in fact a reason must say what differs.
1 mark: the correct idea instead - exact measures such as reinforced frames, deep foundations, trained services and drills.

items.prompt: For an earthquake you have studied, describe two of its main features.
items.canonical_answer: The earthquake that struck Nepal on 25 April 2015 had a magnitude of 7.8, with its focus about 15 kilometres deep beneath Gorkha district, north-west of the capital Kathmandu. Nearly 9,000 people died and thousands more were injured.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all: the date and magnitude; the focus and its location; the death toll; any fact specific to the named earthquake.

items.prompt: For an earthquake you have studied, explain why its effects were so severe.
items.canonical_answer: In Nepal's 2015 earthquake, the shaking was strong because the focus was shallow, about 15 kilometres down, so the energy lost little of its force before reaching the surface. The buildings were weak: many homes and old towers in the Kathmandu valley were brick and mud without reinforced frames, so they collapsed onto the people inside. Landslides then blocked mountain roads, which cut off villages in districts such as Gorkha and Sindhupalchok from rescuers. The monsoon that followed added disease and further landslides, so survivors lost homes, harvests and help at once.
marking_guidance: This example earns 1 mark per developed reason, to 4: the shallow focus near the crowded valley; weak brick-and-mud buildings, so they collapsed; landslides cutting off villages; the monsoon that followed, because each reason is tied to the named earthquake.

items.prompt: For a volcano you have studied, describe two of its main features.
items.canonical_answer: Mount Merapi is a strato-volcano about 30 kilometres north of Yogyakarta on the Indonesian island of Java. Its 2010 eruption, its largest in more than a century, sent pyroclastic flows down the slopes, killed about 350 people and led to the evacuation of around 350,000.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, 2 in all: the type and location; the 2010 pyroclastic flows; the deaths and evacuations; any fact specific to the named volcano.

items.prompt: For a volcano you have studied, explain why people continue to live on its slopes even though it erupts.
items.canonical_answer: On Merapi the ash weathers into unusually fertile soil, so the slopes are farmed densely with vegetables and fruit, because the harvests there are among the best on Java. The mountain also supplies work: sand and stone from its eruptions are dug for building, and visitors who come to see the volcano pay guides and guesthouses. The risk is managed rather than ignored: Indonesia's observatory watches Merapi for earthquake swarms, swelling and gas, so in 2010 around 350,000 people were evacuated before the largest flows, which is why the death toll stayed near 350 rather than in the thousands.
marking_guidance: This example earns 1 mark per developed reason, to 4: fertile ash soil farmed densely; sand, stone and tourism giving work; monitoring and the 2010 evacuation, because each point is carried by the named volcano.

items.prompt: For a named volcano you have studied, describe the hazards it has presented to people and assess how successfully the authorities have responded to them. [7]
items.canonical_answer: Mount Merapi, a strato-volcano about 30 kilometres north of Yogyakarta on the Indonesian island of Java, erupts often, and its hazards are severe: in the 2010 eruption, pyroclastic flows of hot gas, ash and rock swept down the valleys on its southern flank, which killed about 350 people and destroyed whole villages, while ash falls buried crops and closed the airport at Yogyakarta. The authorities responded with success where it mattered most. Scientists at Indonesia's volcano observatory recorded the warning signs - earthquake swarms, swelling ground and rising gas - and ordered evacuations in stages, so around 350,000 people moved off the slopes before the largest flows of 5 November 2010. The death toll of about 350 was far below the losses of the eruptions of earlier centuries. Success was not complete: some people slipped back to tend farms and animals during the eruption and were caught by the flows, so the assessment is that monitoring and evacuation worked, while keeping everyone off the mountain failed.
marking_guidance: Level 1 (1-3): simple statements about volcano hazards, with no named example or only general points about lava and ash.
Level 2 (4-6): developed and linked statements about a named volcano; capped at 5 if no named example is given.

Level 3 (7): comprehensive statements with place-specific detail - Merapi, Yogyakarta, the 2010 pyroclastic flows, the 350,000 evacuated, about 350 deaths - covering hazards and an assessment of the response, developed towards a judgement.

items.prompt:
The table gives details of two earthquakes that happened in 2015:

| | earthquake in Nepal | earthquake in Chile |
|---|---|---|
| magnitude | 7.8 | 8.3 |
| depth of focus | about 15 km | about 25 km |
| people killed | about 9,000 | under 20 |

(a) Identify the more powerful of the two earthquakes. [1]
(b) Describe what the table shows about the number of people killed. [2]
(c) Suggest why the more powerful earthquake killed far fewer people. [3]
(d) Suggest why an earthquake with a deep focus usually causes less damage than one with a shallow focus. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) The earthquake in Chile, at magnitude 8.3 against 7.8 for Nepal.
(b) The table shows a huge contrast: about 9,000 people were killed in Nepal while Chile's deaths were under 20, which means the weaker of the two earthquakes was by far the more deadly.
(c) Chile builds with earthquakes in mind: its buildings use reinforced frames and deep foundations under strict building regulations, so the shaking found fewer weak walls to collapse. Its people practise drills and its emergency services are trained and equipped, which means help arrives quickly. Nepal's Kathmandu valley, by contrast, held many old brick-and-mud buildings that collapsed readily.
(d) Waves from a deep focus travel through more rock before reaching the surface, so their energy spreads and weakens on the way, which means the shaking felt above a deep earthquake is usually gentler than that of a shallow one of the same size.
marking_guidance: Resource: (a) 1 mark for the Chile earthquake read from the table, with the figure 8.3 against 7.8.
Figures: (b) 2 marks for the contrast stated with the values - about 9,000 deaths against under 20.

Marks: (c) 3 marks - building design and regulations, drills and trained emergency services, each developed with its reason; evidence such as Nepal's weak brick-and-mud buildings strengthens the answer.
Evidence: (d) 2 marks - energy spreading through more rock, so the surface shaking is weaker; the depth values in the table may be used as evidence.
